interactionPlan.concept: A periodic ramp (sawtooth) wave can be reconstructed by summing an infinite series of harmonically related sine waves with decreasing amplitudes.
learningObjectives: The student will understand how adding higher-frequency sine waves shapes a smooth wave into a sharp, straight-lined ramp.

The student will be able to explain how the alternating signs and decaying amplitudes of the coefficients ($a_n = (-1)^{n+1}/n$) prevent constructive interference from destroying the linear ramp profile.
The student will observe and identify the Gibbs phenomenon (overshoot) at the sharp discontinuities of the periodic ramp wave.
interactionPlan.keyInsight: By adding infinitely many smooth, rounded sine waves of higher and higher frequencies, we can perfectly reconstruct straight lines and sharp corners.

interactions.label: Number of terms (N)
interactions.effect: Controls the number of harmonic components shown and summed. Increasing N adds higher frequency components to the top plot and updates the combined Fourier reconstruction on the bottom plot, making it visibly closer to a perfect sawtooth wave.
interactions.teaches: How higher frequencies provide the fine-grained spatial detail needed to resolve sharp transitions and straight slopes.

interactions.label: Show target ramp
interactions.effect: Toggles a dashed background reference line representing the ideal periodic ramp function.
interactions.teaches: Allows direct visual comparison of the Fourier approximation's error (ripples and overshoot) against the ideal target signal.

interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: The interface should feature a stacked two-panel layout. The top panel plots the individual component waves ($a_n \sin(nt)$) color-coded differently, up to the selected N. The bottom panel plots the cumulative sum of these components as a bold blue line, overlaid on a light-gray dashed ideal sawtooth wave (period $2\pi$). The X-axis should span from $-3\pi$ to $3\pi$ with ticks at multiples of $\pi$ to clearly demonstrate the periodic nature of the Fourier reconstruction outside the single period interval.
